BORDEN (Prime Minister).,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,QUESTIONS.,PELAGIC SEALING.,,I would like to say to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who asked a question yesterday about the

treaty in reference to pelagic sealing, that I have this further information which I think it is only right that my right hon. friend should have. The Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs informs me that the ratifications in the matter of the pelagic sealing treaty of the 7th July, 1911, were deposited in the United States Department of State on the 12th December, 1911. This procedure is equivalent to an exchange of ratifications. It was thought more convenient for the four powers to deposit their ratifications in the Department of State rather than go through the somewhat complicated procedure of exchanging ratifications with each other.

,Liberal,,Alexander Kenneth Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188&Language=E&Section=ALL
358593,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.5,1912-03-07,15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d,ca.m.5907,Mr. HAZEN.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,The minister will appoint two members of the board. Prof. Prince has been a member of the board in the past and it is likely he will be again appointed. The universities mentioned in the Bill: Dalhousie, Laval, McGill, New Brunswick, Queen's and Toronto, carry on biological work. There is provision _ made in the Bill that when any other university engages in the work of biological research a representative from it may be added to the board.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Douglas Hazen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d&Language=E&Section=ALL
358594,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.6,1912-03-07,56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188,ca.m.519,Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).,,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,Will the two members of the board appointed by the minister, devote all their time to this biological work ?

,Liberal,,Alexander Kenneth Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188&Language=E&Section=ALL
358595,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.7,1912-03-07,15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d,ca.m.5907,Mr. HAZEN.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,By no means; there is no necessity for that. The work of Prof. Prince in the department is in line with the biological work he will do in connection with this board. The other member of the board appointed by the minister will be an official of the department whose business it is to make a study of fishery conditions.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Douglas Hazen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d&Language=E&Section=ALL
358596,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.8,1912-03-07,56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188,ca.m.519,Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).,,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,- I do not wish to make any definite criticism of the constitution of the board, but in my judgment the minister would obtain better results if Mr. BORDEN

some members of the board devoted their whole time to this biological work. Prof. Prince has not been able to devote his whole time to this work in the past, and I have always considered it a mistake that he should have been assigned to work other than that for which he was originally appointed into the service. There is great field for biological work in connection with our fisheries, and Prof. Prince might with advantage to the country, devote his time exclusively to that work. I do not, of course, object to representatives of the universities being appointed, but still they can only be an auxiliary force and can hardly be considered practical working members of this board. I trust the minister will see that in future Prof. Prince shall devote his entire time to this particular work, and probably it would be well to associate one or two permanent officers with him.

,Liberal,,Alexander Kenneth Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188&Language=E&Section=ALL
358597,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.9,1912-03-07,d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2,ca.m.9083,Mr. SINCLAIR.,,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,The minister must not forget the practical side of the work of this board, and I may say that up to this date the board has not done very much practical work for our fisheries. Recently, Professor Prince gave evidence before the Fisheries Committee and he explained that owing to the fact that the gentlemen who composed the board were not salaried, the department was not in a position to give them instructions to do any special work, which I regard as a very important feature of this whole matter. There are many practical questions which arise in connection with the fisheries, and which a board of this kind ought to be able to solve. Tihe scientific side of the question is all right and I have no criticism to offer on the work which the university professors are doing, but most of it is I suppose in connection with their professional duties in their colleges, which of course it is right the department should aid them in. There are a great many questions in dispute among practical fishermen which this board could do a good deal to throw light upon. A few days ago the question of steam trawling was under discussion in the House, and the minister appeared to think that it was not destructive to our fisheries, while I, like many others who live on the sea-coast, take an entirely different view. If we were able to refer such a question to the board and have them make actual investigation as is done in Great Britain where they employ vessels of their own in that service, it would be of great benefit to our fisheries. Then, as to the propagation of lobsters; the Fisheries Department has placed a great many millions of young lobsters in the sea year after year, and there is a variety of opinion amongst fishermen as to whether they ever mature. I do not think it would be very difficult for scientists to discover exactly what pro-

gress these lobsters make 'after they are put in the water. I urge on the minister the necessity of appointing a first-class practical man on this board who will get a salary and devote his whole time to the work.

,Liberal,,John Howard Sinclair,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2&Language=E&Section=ALL
358598,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.10,1912-03-07,15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d,ca.m.5907,Mr. HAZEN.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,As to the desirability of some members of this commission giving their entire time to the duties devolving upon them, I may point out that there are biological stations in different parts of Canada where during the season observations are taken from day to day in regard to matters that are of interest to this biological board.

Observers are placed at these stations for the purpose of making accurate records of the observations so taken. The results of those observations are furnished to the members of this board, and from these, and such observations as they may make themselves, conclusions are arrived at which may be valuable. These observations are, of course, made under the direction of this board, which at the present time is vested with greater powers of management than it had before. While the officials appointed under the board are to be paid, the board itself acts in an advisory capacity, and is charged with the management of these stations and the carrying on of this work. If the results of the work carried on by the Biological Board are found to be beneficial, it will have to be carried on upon a permanent scale; and, if so, it will become more expensive, and a larger sum of money will be required to carry it on than the modest sum voted by parliament in the past. The work will probably be one of growth and development. I think the suggestions made by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), who takes a very active and intelligent interest in all fishery matters, are well worthy of consideration. I shall have great pleasure in directing the attention of the Biological Board to the suggestion of my hon. friend that more practical work should be done under its direction. There are in the department to-day officials whose duty it is to consider these fishery questions from a practical standpoint. My experience has been that it is difficult to get fishery experts to agree, and it is very seldom that they agree on technical questions. I suppose there is room for a divergence of opinion, because after the fish leaves the shores and gets into deep water, very little is known of its habits. My hon. friend, in referring to steam trawling, rather inferred that I considered that it was not destructive. If my remarks conveyed that impression, it is contrary to what I intended them to convey. I think that steam trawling is undoubtedly destructive in its ef-145$

fects, from the fact that many more fish are destroyed by that method than by other methods. My hon. friend also referred to the work done by the lobster hatcheries, and raised the question whether the conditions under which the lobsters were being hatched and cared for while very young are such as will enable them to live and increase the lobster industry of the country. I know that there is a great difference of opinion on this subject. There are some who believe that the young lobsters are not sufficiently protected under the present system, and that another system should be adopted. Others take the opposite view. This is a subject which we are trying to work out with the view of arriving at the correct solution. I will take up the suggestion of my hon. friend with the chairman of the Biological Board, and see if it will not be possible, besides giving attention to the scientific aspect of the question, to give attention also to the practical side.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Douglas Hazen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d&Language=E&Section=ALL
358599,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.11,1912-03-07,56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188,ca.m.519,Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).,,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,Unless there are certain officers in the department who can devote their entire time to biological work, there is very little use in creating a biological board. This work has been very much neglected in the past. But I rise for the purpose of suggesting to the hon. minister that instead of a biological board there should be a fisheries board, consisting of officers of his own department and certain other persons living in the different provinces and interested in fisheries. I fear that such of his officers as are supposed to devote their time to the fisheries are so fully occupied with matters of a general character that they can hardly be expected to do good work along special lines. I think it would be a very good departure if the department were to organize a fisheries board, with the biological board as a branch of that board, the two Working together. I know that the suggestion has frequently been made, in the province of Nova Scotia at least, and probably it has been conevyed to the minister since he came into office. I have often heard the suggestion made myself, and I have always looked on it with considerable favour. I think the departmental officers would receive a great deal of assistance by working together with appointees from the various provinces interested, and I would like the minister to take this into consideration terore the next session of parliament.

,Liberal,,Alexander Kenneth Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188&Language=E&Section=ALL
358600,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.6.12,1912-03-07,15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d,ca.m.5907,Mr. HAZEN.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service,QUESTIONS.,BIOLOGICAL BOARD OF CANADA.,,The suggestion which my hon. friend makes is, in my judgment, well worthy of serious consideration. I do not think the suggestion is a new one. I think it has been made in this House before, when the estimates of the Fisheries Department have been under consideration. Fisheries boards, I understand, exist in

other countries. There is one, I believe, in England, and one in Scotland, and these boards have been instrumental in doing a great deal lor the conservation of the fishery interests in those countries. There is force in what my hon. friend says about the fisheries officials of the department having their time taken up with general matters and not being able to give as much time as should be given to problems of importance in connection with the fishing wealth of Canada.

I have found in the Marine Department that the Lighthouse Board is a most useful body, and one which not only relieves the minister of responsibility-perhaps I should not put that forward as a .reason, because the minister is bound to take the responsibility-but which furnishes advice concerning the aids to navigation, the lighthouses, and the protection of our coasts, that is of very great value, and which it would be difficult to deal with in any other way. I may say-and I am saying it without a thorough study of the subject-that it certainly seemed to me that a board constituted along the same lines for the purpose of advising on questions affecting the fisheries, fisheries protection, the fishery patrol service, close seasons and open seasons, and the implements and means employed in the catching of fish, might be of very great use and assistance to the minister in charge of the department and to the country as well. I have been giving some thought to the matter-I cannot say that I have arrived at a conclusion, I have not the knowledge at present sufficient to enable me to do so-but it is mv intention to give very careful consideration to the matter between this session and the next session of parliament.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Douglas Hazen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=15b270da-620f-48bb-be53-9255fee3838d&Language=E&Section=ALL

358624,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.7.20,1912-03-07,e2f3ce71-bd81-4d34-8a08-56a140552231,ca.m.3549,Sir WILFRID LAURIER.,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS.,YUKON JUDGES.,,With regard to the payment to Mr. Newcombe, my recollection is that my hon. friend is some-Mr. DOHERTY.

what in error as to his facts. It is quite true that Sir Oliver Mowat, the first Minister of Justice under the late administration, certified an account to be paid to Mr. Newcombe, but that was an account for services which had been rendered under the previous administration, and of course the following Ministers of Justice certified to accounts for services rendered since we came into office, but the basis of the claim of Mr. Newcombe was an alleged agreement that when he took office under the previous administration he had stipulated that he would be allowed to practice and to perform such services as he did afterwards. I do not wish to put in controversy the work done by Mr. Newcombe who is a very good lawyer, an efficient Deputy Minister and a gentleman whose word must be taken, but it was, to say the-least of it, an extraordinary piece of business that an agreement of that kind should be made by the minister of the day without there being any record of it. Moreover, I do not think that such an agreement could have been binding or legal and as to this I would appeal to the judgment of Mr. Newcombe himself. I would have preferred that my hon. friend had done as we did and left Mt. Newcombe to his recourse in law, an appeal to the Exchequer Court.

My hon. friend has chosen to do what the late government would not do. I think there was no cause whatever to make such a payment to Mr. Newcombe. The reason why we did not accept this agreement was the reason which was afterwards embodied in the statute, that no member of the civil service should receive any remuneration beyond his salary. If that was ' not the law in 1892, or 1893, when Mr. Newcombe was appointed, it was the spirit of the law, and, for these reasons, I think my hon. friend would be better advised if he left Mr. Newcombe to his recourse in the Court of Exchequer.

358628,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.7.24,1912-03-07,52a4499f-fa60-4960-92e4-bb99baf0c85e,ca.m.8507,Mr. TURRIFF.,,QUESTIONS.,YUKON JUDGES.,,The Minister of Justice points out that these judges are appointed for life. I understand that the living allowance of $5,000 that they have been receiving in the past, is not a life matter. That was granted at the time because living in the Yukon was very expensive. I am quite satisfied that if my hon, friend wants these gentlemen, who are capable men and who are still young men, to take hold of other work, all he has to do is to drop off the living allowance and they will be pleased, 1 am sure, to take up work in other parts of the Dominion. With reference to the defence that the Minister of Justice makes for paying these large sums to the deputy Minister of Justice, surely it must have appeared to him that, if this account had been hanging fire for so many years, although it had been recommended by three or four Ministers of Justice, there must have been some good reason why it was not paid. What does the deputy minister get his salary for, if it is not to do the work of the department? It seems a very strange proceeding; Why should one deputy minister, who is paid an extra salary anyway, be allowed to charge for work done for his own department? Would you allow any other deputy minister to charge for the work that he does in his denaTt-niient, outside of his own salary? The Minister of Justice must have known that the late government had refused to pay that account, He must have known that, there was some good ground for not paying that account. Here we have an official getting $7,000 a year and all his expenses when he travels over to the old country in connection with the work of the department and it is a remarkable thing that he should be allowed to draw big fees and in addition

be paid his expenses while he is over there pleading cases for private parties. It seems to me to be a very strange thing that just as soon as this government come in they pay this amount that the late government refused to pay. However, the Minister of Justice must take the responsibility for that payment, but it will be pretty difficult to justify it to a great many people in the country, who do not earn anything like $7,000 a year, to whom $7,000 a year and all expenses seems a pretty good salary, equal to the salary of the Minister of Justice and of all his colleagues except the Prime Minister of Canada. ,Liberal,,John Gillanders Turriff,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=52a4499f-fa60-4960-92e4-bb99baf0c85e&Language=E&Section=ALL
358629,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.7.25,1912-03-07,9796aa93-03f8-4d49-ac6a-f2eab36fbe1c,ca.m.3478,Mr. THOMPSON (Yukon).,,QUESTIONS.,YUKON JUDGES.,,Just before the resolution is adopted, I would like to offer an explanation as to the cause which gave rise to the necessity for this measure. When the Yukon was first settled in 1896, after the discovery of the Klondike, there were no laws governing placer mining in that country. Placer mining as an industry did not obtain to any considerable extent in Canada up to that time. There were some placer mines, but they were in provinces which had laws previous to the time that these provinces had entered confederation, such as British Columbia. That necessitated the making of laws governing the placer mining industry in the Yukon Territory, and for several years after the discovery of gold in 1896 the industry was governed altogether, not by laws, but by orders in council. There was a very great inrush I of people to the goldfields, a great many | claims were staked, boundaries overlapped and as a result a very great deal of litigation arose. The courts, in the first few years of the existence of the territory as a territory, were overworked. Subsequently all these regulations were gathered together, assorted and passed upon by the people of the territory, finally brought to parliament and passed through parlia-parliament as the Yukon Placer Act, thus placing the chief industry of the Yukon on a more solid, permanent and better basis. As a result of that Act a great deal of the cause of the litigation of earlier years was removed. The . consequence was that, although we had practically the same population, we had less litigation because our laws were in a better condition. The appeal was formerly from the Yukon court to the court in British Columbia, but after the court of the territory was established with three judges, appeals lay in Dawson city itself. The fortunes of a mining country like the

Yukon may fluctuate and at the present moment I regret to say that we have not as many people in the Yukon as we had when that court was established. That, however, is not a criterion as to the future of the territory, as we hope, and we have every reason to believe, that before many years, we shall have as many people and perhaps more than we have had and that the fortunes of the Yukon will be improved. Many new finds have been made and other prospects are looming up, all of which lead to the hope, based upon the history of mining in past years, that we will have a population in the Yukon requiring this full court. There is in this Bill a clause which provides for the recall of these judges. By passing this measure the country'saves $10,000 per year, and if we find that we have to reconstitute this court we may recall these two judges who are to be retired.

358634,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.8.3,1912-03-07,0e4f9dca-5c4f-43d7-af07-16546fe9215d,ca.m.2882,Mr. REID.,Minister of Customs,QUESTIONS.,CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT.- CUSTOMS OUTSIDE SERVICE.,,This is a copy of a Bill introduced last session by the Hon. Mr. Paterson, my predecessor in office, and which was not passed owing_ to the dissolution. The Bill proposes to increase the salaries of some of the officers in the outside customs service such, as the collectors of ports and chief clerks. 'We introduce a class called senior chief clerks with a salary ranging from $2,200 to $2,800, and who will be employed only in the large cities like Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg. The present system is to have a chief clerk for each department at these ports, but the business is so increasing that it has been found necessary to have a senior oflicial over these clerks who must be a man of experience in the service and be the very best officer we can find in the port. The surveyors now get from $1,200 to $2,400 a year, and the Bill proposes to make the maximum $2,800. The assistant surveyors now get from $800 to $1,200, and in future they^ will get from $1,200 to $1,600. We provide for new officials called Dominion appraisers, who will receive a salary ranging from $2,200 to $2,600. At present we have an appraiser for each department, but we want a man at each large port who Mr. THOMPSON (Yukon).

will see that the appraisers do their work properly and are qualified for the position. The Dominion appraiser will act as inspector of the other appraisers. Then we are introducing a new class called senior clerks whose salaries will range from $1,200 to $1,600. 358642,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.8.11,1912-03-07,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,QUESTIONS.,CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT.- CUSTOMS OUTSIDE SERVICE.,,As I understand1, a sub-collector is one who is required to report to a collector near by. For instance, the city of Moncton has a collector, and there are sub-collectors at Shediae, Hillsborough, in Albert county and Dorchester, who are subject to the jurisdiction and the control of the collector at Moncton. At the outports where these sub-collectors are placed the revenues as a rule are not large, though the export business is somewhat large and there may be a great deal of shipping. For instance, at Hillsborough, in Albert county, there is an immense amount of shipping of plaster and other raw material, which is quarried and shipped to the United States and1 other countries. The imports at that port are comparatively small, and yet the sub-collector there is required to be in his office at all times during office hours, and his salary is certainly not commensurate with the time he has to devote to his official duties. The same is true of Baie Verte and Cape Tormentine,. and other ports which are sub-ports of Sackville. In years past, when I felt called upon to interview the predecessor of my hon. friend in office, his uniform reply was that, regardless of the duties a man had to perform or the time he had to devote to those duties, the amount of revenue collected was the governing principle in fixing his salary. Now, I would strongly urge my hon. friend to make a reform in this matter. Take the collector at the port of Moncton, which has a population of 14,000 or 15,000. Under his jurisdiction are sub-collectors at Hillsborough, Cocaigne, Shediae, and Dorchester. He is responsible in a large measure for the oversight of these several suboffices. It does seem to me that $1,400 or $1,500 is a paltry salary to give to a man holding such a responsible position. At the port of Sackville the salary is, I think, $800 or $900. Yet these officers are required to be in attendance at their offices) during office hours, and1 oftentimes outside of office hours, in order to clear vessels so as to enable them to take advantage of the tide. If the hon. minister will inquire into the matter, I think he will realize that these officials have been in the past underpaid, and that a remedy should be applied. I hold that the criterion of a man's salary should not be the revenue of his office. Some of the most important ports in the province of New Brunswick, and also in the province of Nova Scotia, are ports where no great amount of importing is done, and1 where the officials are engaged in attending to export business. In these days the large importations into this country are made at the great centres, such as Montreal, Halifax, Quebec and other shipping ports. But the smaller ports are a necessity in the interests of

navigation, and in the interests of trade and commerce. Officials are necessary, their time must be devoted to the duties of their offices, and they should be paid on a scale larger than has heretofore prevailed1.

I would urge upon the attention of my hon. friend this feature of the question of salaries. I do not observe that under this Bill any particular provision is made for officials of that class, but I think there should be. It seems that these provisions are intended to apply to the larger ports of Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, St. John and Halifax. But the smaller ports of the country should also receive attention. Take the one to which my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) referred, the important port of Woodstock, being on the border of the United States the officials there are necessarily continuously applying themselves to their duties. The same can be said of Moncton, which is a centre, Charlottetown and other similar points. The officials at these places are not provided for by this Bill, if I read it aright, and it seems to me that the collectors and sub-collectors, particularly _ the latter, should be recognized. I believe it to have been the policy of the department in later years to combine a number of ports together under the control of one official who is known as the collector, the other officials being designated sub-collectors. And these collectors and sub-collectors certainly have important duties. I invite my hon. friend's favourable consideration to the point raised.

358670,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.8.39,1912-03-07,80f4de9d-1b1a-4db1-93cf-9cb7b9b63dd4,ca.m.9843,Mr. CARVELL.,,QUESTIONS.,CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT.- CUSTOMS OUTSIDE SERVICE.,,I quite approve of this Bill and I concur in the remarks that have been made as to the great difficulty any minister must have in a department of this kind in satisfying and at the same time doing justice to a horde of officials. the honour to represent, must he constantly on the alert to guard against the very frequent cases of petty smuggling. Collector "" means the collector of the customs at the port or place intended, or any person lawfully deputed, appointed, or authorized to do the duty of collector thereat.

358682,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.8.51,1912-03-07,d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2,ca.m.9083,Mr. SINCLAIR.,,QUESTIONS.,CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT.- CUSTOMS OUTSIDE SERVICE.,,The dismissal appears to have been based upon a letter written by this Mr. Lyman Smith. There* are three letters in the correspondence, one to the Prime Minister, one to the Minister of Customs, and the third to Mr. Smith, member for that constituency. I have been unable to find anything in Mr. Lyman Smith's letter to justify his dismissal, I will read it:
Ottawa, November 21, 1911. Hon. Dr. J. D. Reid, M.P.,
Minister of Customs,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I have received the following from Mr. Lyman Smith, collector of customs, Ottawa, viz.:-
' Oshawa, Nov. 15, 1911.
' William Smith, Esq., M.P.,
' House of Commons,
' Ottawa, Ont.

'Dear Sir,-The 'Indicator' to-day reports that at a meeting in Oshawa at which you were present, Dr. Raiser said I should be removed from office as an offensive partisan. I have thought best to give you a plain statement of facts:
' (1) I was not appointed because of political services.
' (2) I never contributed a cent for any election.
' (3) I never even sat on any political platform in my life.
' (4) I never spoke at any meeting.
' (5) I never was in a party committee room in my life, nor attended any such meeting.
' (6) I never canvassed for votes, nor spoke to any man with any intention of influencing his vote.
' (7) I attended four political meetings- two on each side. I took no part in any demonstration. I never even cheered for any candidate or speaker.
' (8) As the eleotion was the one subject of conversation, I conversed with perhaps a dozen whom I chanced to meet, and expressed my views of the question at issue.

' (9) I hold certain views in regard to the conduct of elections and expressed these views to private parties and only in private conversation. I did not hesitate to express them, but it was with no intention of influencing votes. I spoke to both friends and opponents.

' (10) I do not believe in canvassing for votes. I do not believe in a party fund. The bare expenses of hiring halls, printing, and such absolute needs, should be met, and I think, by the State, for all legitimate expenses are for the good of the country or should be. I do not think voters should be carried to the poll, except old and feeble folk, and the expense of this should be borne by the state. I do not believe in parades or demonstrations. I never took part in one. I think there should be open and fair discussion. Public meetings should be held to inform the people of the questions at issue, then the voters should go quietly to the polls of their own accord and exercise their franchise without fear or favour.

' (11) The head and front of my offending seems to be that I stated to John McCulloch that I considered the right of the franchise so sacred that I would never vote for any man, no matter who he was, or what party, or what the issue, who had proved to have been concerned in the giving of money for bribes. I stated that I had on a few occasions unknowingly voted for such, but I would never so vote if I knew it. Tf pure men did not offer themselves I would not vote at all. I further stated that in my opinion a man that had done this should not have a vote himself, or be permitted to hold any office. This view Mr. SINCLAIR.
was stated in general terms, and I have often, made the same statement when an election was pending. Remember, please, that all this was said in private conversation only.
' I know that customs officers are supposed to take no part in politics; but I judged we lived not in Russia but in Canada, where a man could express his views privately to his friends.

' I have done nothing that I wish to deny or conceal. I never considered you anything but a friend, and was persuaded you entertained like feelings towards me. Therefore, there could be no personal animus in this matter. It was merely a statement of my principles.
' I am, dear sir,
' Yours truly,
(Sgd.) LYMAN C. SMITH.

Mr. Smith was appointed to the customs of Oshawa about a year ago, and in many ways was very active during the eleotion which closed on September 21. I think the above letter would be all that was necessary to cause his removal, which I would recommend to be done as soon as possible.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) WILLIAM SMITH.
The answer of the Minister to Mr. Lyman Smith's letter, was as follows:
Ottawa, 6th Dec., 1911. Lyman C. Smith, Esq., B.A.,
Acting collector of Customs,
Oshawa, Ont.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 2nd inet., respecting a charge of partisanship against you, and have carefully noted your representations in the matter.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) ,T. D. REID, Minister of Customs.
The Prime Minister appears to have

turned the letter addressed to him which is almost an exact copy of the letter to Win. Smith, M.P., over to the Minister of Customs, and the next one is a letter from Mr. John McDougald, the Commissioner of Customs, to Mr. Lyman Smits, as follows: Ottawa, 27th Dec., 1911. Lyman C. Smith, Esq.,
Acting Commissioner of Customs,
Oshawa, Ont.

Sir,-In my letter of 80th December, 1910, authorizing your employment as acting collector of customs at Oshawa, Ont., it was stipulated that this employment may be discontinued at any time at the discretion of the Minister of Customs.

I am now directed to inform you, by order of the Minister of Customs, that, on account of political partisanship, your employment as acting collector of customs will be discontinued and shall terminate on the 30th December, 1911, at the close of which day you will deliver the books and other customs property in your charge to the Inspector of Customs who hands you this letter.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) JOHN McDOUGALD, Commissioner of Customs.

Now, there is nothing whatever in that letter of Mr. Lyman Smith which seems to justify his dismissal. I do not know the circumstances more than what appears in the correspondence, but this man was certainly not a partisan. According to his own story he is an extraordinary man; he does not seem to have taken the usual interest that men everywhere take in public affairs, and he appears to be under the impression himself that he was dismissed because he made the statement that he did not approve of bribery at elections. Surely that would not be a good reason for dismissing this official, and that is the reason which appears to have been acted upon in this case after having read the correspondence, I ask the minister to give an explanation.

,Liberal,,John Howard Sinclair,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2&Language=E&Section=ALL

358701,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.8.70,1912-03-07,0d105fac-7cfa-4e90-8130-9904481a8b80,ca.m.3779,Mr. MARTIN (Regina).,,QUESTIONS.,CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT.- CUSTOMS OUTSIDE SERVICE.,,I approve of the principle of increasing the salaries of the officers mentioned in this Bill. This Bill refers particularly to collectors and inspectors and makes provision for the payment to them of such salaries as will be adequate and sufficient to keep them in a reasonable way. By so doing I believe you will attract better men into the civil service of the country. But there is- a class of government officials throughout the country whose needs I submit, are just as great as the needs of the inspectors, collectors and inspectors of customs throughout the country, and even greater, I refer to the' ordinary customs officials, for instance in the office of Regina, or in the customs offices in similar cities and towns in western Canada, and I believe the same argument will apply to towns in eastern Canada although perhaps not to so great an extent. The cost of living in western Canada, as well as in eastern Canada, has increased tremendously. I know instances of customs officials resident in Canada to-day who are not getting sufficient allowance to actually subsist upon. I submit that is not a fair position to put any government official in. The revenue of this country is vastly in excess of the current expenditure at the present time, and I think that part, of that surplus might very well be expended by the government in making a general increase to the civil service, if not in the actual salary at least in the living allowance. The living allowance granted in the west to .many of these officials is certainly not adequate. My own experience in connection with government offices in western Canada has been that the only man who can he got to enter a government position, outside of the better class of offices, is a man who is temporarily out of employment, and who says: I will go into the position for two or three months in the hope of getting something better outside and then I will leave the service. If you want ability in the government service throughout the whole of Canada, if you wish to secure efficient and capable men who will devote their lives to the service of the government, you must pay them salaries adequate to their positions and equal to the salaries they can obtain in similar employment elsewhere Mr. BORDEN.

I think at the present time we are not paying sufficient .salaries to the ordinary clerks throughout the country. Take for instance in my own part of the country, the wages paid in every calling in life, from the ordinary labourer up, have increased during the past three or four years, and increased adequately with the cost of living in the west. The only calling in which the remuneration has not been increased has been in the civil service of Canada. I recognize, of course, that the class of men to whom I am calling the attention of the House do not come under the provisions of this Bill. At the same time I would ask the Minister of Customs to direct his attention to the ordinary customs officials throughout the country, and if possible give them adequate salaries to live upon. In the city of Regina it would take (half the salary obtained by the average customs clerk to pay the rent of an ordinary house, and that is not a fair position to put these officials in.

358736,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.10.4,1912-03-07,5afbdf71-2ff3-4501-b9b3-74750bfc73ee,ca.m.7078,Mr. TURGEON.,,QUESTIONS.,EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES- MANITOBA.,,Mr. Chairman, 1 wish to be permitted to say a few words of appreciation of the statements made and the sentiments expressed by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) when he moved his amendment yesterday. This amendment does not interfere with the operation of the Bill. It is only requesting that the grant made, or offered to the province of Manitoba in connection with this extension of territory be delayed for a while until the suggested conference shall have been . held. We are not asking you to take away anything from the amount allotted by the government; we are only asking that further consideration of the general question may be given by such a conference. There nas been a tendency during this debate to allege that Liberal speakers who have presented objeotions to this proposition now before the committee have displayed a spirit of reluctance to allow the people of Manitoba the full enjoyment of what they are entitled to. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, and every member of this House, as I can assure the whole country, that no man in the maritime provinces regrets the 1464

prosperity of Manitoba or any other prairie province. No man has more admiration for the people of Manitoba, who-se activity, intellectual as well as physical, seems to be stimulated and enlivened by the invigorating atmosphere which pervades the country in which they have made their homes. The people of the maritime provinces have generously contributed to the purchase of these western territories fox the common welfare of the Dominion and it is gratifying to us to see that our children have gone forth from Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to assist in
column2: the development of that great

column1: west, have reflected credit upon their native provinces, and that those of them who have been elected to represent their fellowmen, young or old, are to be found in the first rank among the members of this parliament. Certainly I wish to insist upon this point that, whatever position may be taken or whatever suggestion may be made, it is always in the spirit of the greatest liberality of the east towards the west. No greater builders of this nation have been in this parliament than the great men from New Brunswick or the illustrious Howe, who foresaw sixty years ago in that great western country what we have realized to-d'ay and whose hopes in regard to that rich heritage have been fulfilled Jo a greater degree than even he could possibly have expected they would be.

A suggestion has been made by my hon. friend from St. John that this Bill should stand until we have a conference of the Premiers of the provinces to consider the rights of the other provinces in connections with this increase in subsidy-it is nothing else-given to Manitoba. I have always been a generous admirer pf the constitution. It is our admiration of the constitution which has made -the people of New Brunswick as good1 Canadians as they have been. We have suffered, in so far as the Catholic minority is concerned, from the terms of confederation, but our sufferings perhaps have only rendered dearer to us that constitution which we cherish today knowing that it will ever stand for the rights which have been acquired in every part of the Dominion. This Bill to-d'ay is merely a usurpation of the rights given at the last provincial conference to the different provinces. There had been an agitation going on for years amongst the provinces to secure an increase in the subsidies in order to enable the provincial governments to better administer the affairs and1 develop the resources under their control. We all know that with the increased revenue of this government the provinces have increased expenditure, and, therefore, it was nothing but natural that

the amount of money fixed by the Fathers of Confederation should be insufficient to meet the present day needs of the provinces. A conference was called by the then leader of the government, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), to meet in 1906, and the provinces were allotted a certain amount each according to the unanimous resolution which was passed. As I stated a few days ago, I regret that this amount was not made larger, because I feel that the time will soon come when th'e provinces will have to come again and ask for a further increase of these subsidies which at present are not sufficient to enable them to administer their many departments according to the needs of the time. I would have expected that this government, when enlarging the territory of Manitoba, and giving an increased subsidy to that province, would1 again have called a conference of the provinces to consider this question of the increase of subsidies together with many other questions in connection with the development of Canada. We have, as I said a moment ago, contributed very spontaneously and generously to any assistance that the west may have required in the past.

We are willing to-day or at any time to contribute for further railways, or for the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, for the great benefit of Ontario and the west. We shall tax ourselves with pleasure whenever any government may be disposed to impose on Canada any expenditure for our national development, which will contribute to the welfare of the people of the west as well as of the people of the east. Meanwhile right is right, and while we are willing always to be generous, we have at the same time to consider our ovra future.

A great deal has been said by my hon. friend the .Minister of the Interior about the province of Manitoba looking like a postage stamp on the map of the Dominion. New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island together are perhaps a still smaller postage stamp on the map of the Dominion. In the meantime, we are not less hopeful of the future; but it may be that such considerations will develop in the minds of the people of the maritime provinces a desire to state as forcibly as possible their position. We have contributed to the purchase of the territories which are now to be allotted to the largest and perhaps the wealthiest provinces of this Dominion. Those territories may become very valuable. If we are to believe half of what we are told in the reports on the resources of northern Ontario and of Ungava, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec will soon get the benefit of territories .as wealthy as any portion of the

358739,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.10.7,1912-03-07,5afbdf71-2ff3-4501-b9b3-74750bfc73ee,ca.m.7078,Mr. TURGEON.,,QUESTIONS.,EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES- MANITOBA.,,Yes, without success. I admire his way of putting the case, and I believe he is convinced that the time has come for a conference of the Premiers of the provinces to settle many of the questions to which he has referred, such as the decreasing representation of. the maritime provinces in this parliament from census to census. On this question my views have not always been similar to those expressed by the hon. minister and by the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Pugs-ley). As I have said, I am a jealous admirer of the constitution, and at the risk even of losing something, I prefer to hold to the fundamental principles of the constitution. Meanwhile, just because at this moment there are divergent opinions as to what step should be taken by the maritime provinces on the question of representation, I say that it is imperative upon the Premiers of the various provinces to come together in order to see what can be done in that regard. I have held during my whole lifetime that it is better for us to stand by the terms of the constitution than to expose ourselves to the danger of tinkering with it. But a conference of the provincial Premiers is the only tribunal before which such a question could be placed to advantage, whatever their de-

cision might""be; and if perchance they could not come to an agreement by which the representation of the maritime provinces should remain in statu quo, or be placed in the position in which it was at the time of confederation, the Premiers of the maritime provinces and the ministers representing those provinces in this government should insist on some financial return in order to place our local governments in a better position to develop their own resources, and thus keep our population at home and bring more population which would enable us to maintain and increase our representation. I have always held the view that just because we have not been in a position to develop our resources as they should be developed, we have not been able to keep the population that has been going away from year to year, until according to the last census the province of New Brunswick shows an increase of only 20,000-increase solely due to the French population.

I regret to see that in the southern counties of New Brunswick the English speaking people have year after year since confederation been drifting towards the New England States, and all on account of that want of development of our agricultural resources which would have kept the children of New Brunswick on their native soil. I support the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley), because I feel the time has come for us to make a fresh start with greater vitality than has actuated us in the past; the time has come for better terms for the provinces and for improving the financial relations with the Dominion of the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. I have many a time advocated in this House greater transportation facilities for the maritime provinces, and I have advocated the construction of a tunnel between Prince Edward Island and the mainland so as to place the population of that fertile island on the same footing as the people of the rest of the Dominion, thus giving greater opportunities to the young men of Prince Edward Island to stay at home on their fertile soil which is capable of sustaining a population of 300,000, and which now, I regret to say, has a population of only

column2: I congratulate the Minister of Railways on promising to establish a car-ferry service between the mainland and the island, but I still believe that the construction of a tunnel, even though we should have to make large sacrifices, would be far more advantageous to the people of the island, and would not in the course of years be any greater burden on our resources. Though I am sure the Minister of Railways will keep his promise with regard to the car-ferry service, I hope to see the day when that tunnel will be constructed. Then again, the question of the representation of the maritime provinces in this parliament must be dealt with, and when we consider that these provinces are decreasing in influence decade after decade in this parliament, it is a matter which must be regretted by every member of this House. Then again, I believe that Newfoundland should he brought into the Canadian union. It may be that the leading statesmen of Newfoundland will not today entertain the idea of uniting with the people of Canada, but there was a time when the stand taken by Newfoundland towards the Dominion was very different, and there may grow up in time to come a feeling in that ancient colony for union with our confederacy. We must not forget that at confederation Newfoundland offered her vast natural resources in agriculture, in lumber, in minerals and in fisheries, to the Dominion, and that unfortunately this offer was not accepted on the terms proposed. Then again in 1895, when the government of Newfoundland came to Ottawa and again offered the resources of their colony to the Dominion, for the sake of a paltry half-million dollars they were permitted to go back without their offer being accepted, and again another fatal mistake was made, by us. Let us not forget that Canada can never become a great nation, unless there is included within the confederation the ancient colony of Newfoundland which occupies such a splendid strategic position at the entrance to the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I trust this government will make every reasonable effort to induce Newfoundland to cast in her lot with us. Perhaps there is an opportunity now that we are inaugurating a naval service for asking Newfoundland to join with us. The Minister of the Naval Service has told us recently that the navy such as we have it to-day will remain, and that until he can confer with the admiralty during the vacation the vessels would be used in the fishery protection service. I trust that after the hon. gentleman does confer with the British authorities, he will return to Canada and be able to announce a naval policy in the interests of the Dominion and of the empire.

column1: But I take advantage of this opportunity to say also that before the hon. gentleman goes to Great Britain, before he confers with the British Admiralty in order to effect a change in the navai system of the late government, which was adopted after a consultation with the British Admiralty and on their advice a year or two ago-although I have no objection to further consultation with and further advice from, the naval authorities in London-would it not be proper for him to listen to my suggestion this even-

ing? Then when he goes to London he will be able to say that he is acting after a conference with the representatives of Newfoundland, the representatives of that great British colony-perhaps the most British colony under the Union Jack where no doubt as to loyalty can be said to exist. For I am sure if he has to establish any naval service at all which would be valuable to Canada and to the empire on the Atlantic coast, the same would also be serviceable to the island of Newfoundland, and would save that colony the large amount of money which she has to pay for the protection of her coasts. The concurrence of Newfoundland would be a most valuable factor. There is no doubt that the union of Newfoundland with Canada is about to come. It is her ultimate destiny, and while the movement for confederation is not a popular one at present in that island, still I have faith that if Canada persists in the policy of conciliation towards Newfoundland that desirable result will yet be accomplished. It behoves Canada, however, to make the first step towards union. The occasion is opportune on the creation of a navy, or the creation of a system, the details of which are not known to us, but which must be made efficient in the interests of Canada and Newfoundland, as well as of the British Empire as a whole. At such a' time would it not be well to unite with Newfoundland and take advantage of the fine strategic position of that island lying as it does at the very gateway of the northern part of the continent. I have already said that I have always been a zealous admirer of the constitution. I heard with pleasure the leader of the government speak last night of the harmonious feeling which exists in the province of Nova Scotia, where there are no statutory separate school systems, but where every child in the province enjoys the system of education there on a footing of equality. Let me say that I commend this spirit of harmony which prevails in Nova Scotia, and which also prevails in the province of New Brunswick. In the latter province we at one time thought we enjoyed a separate school system which was statutory, so strong was our faith in the legality of that school system at that time. The leader of the government will admit that the harmony which may prevail in any one or two provinces in regard to school matters does not curtail a constitutional right with respect to schools possessed by any section of people in other provinces. Therefore, it is not merely on the fact that a spirit of harmony exists in the maritime provinces that we should build up our hopes for the future. It is well known that the fathers of eonfedera-Mr. TURGEON.

tion had intended to give the maritime provinces separate schools the same as in Ontario and Quebec, but we did not get them. The words ' by law ' having been introduced into the Act of Confederation, with respect to the school system, it was found that our schools, although they were advantageous did not give us the rights we thought we possessed. Those rights, it seems, were enjoyed by practice but not by law. The troubles of the past in New Brunswick in regard to the school question are well known. I have taken an active part in public life myself and participated in these troubles; and it is on that account, as I said a while ago, that I have learned to admire the constitution. We found ourselves by the decision of the Privy Council confirming the judgment of the supreme court of New Brunswick, in this position: We did not have separate schools by law, and the privileges we had been enjoying were only given to us by practice. If you consider the settlement which was made in regard to the province of Manitoba, you will see how very carefully that great statesman Sir John A. Macdonald acted at that time. By reason of his experience of the situation in New Brunswick he was careful in framing the constitution for Manitoba to insert into the constitution the words ' by law or by practice,' hoping therefore to avoid in the case of the minority in Manitoba the troubles which had arisen in the province of New Brunswick. Again contrary to the interpretation of the law it was once more found that in that western territory, including the province of Manitoba, there did not legally exist separate schools, and therefore it was left to the local legislature of the new province to enact whatever statute it might see fit in regard to education. But it is well known that a system of separate schools, which was agreeable to the majority as well as to the minority, was introduced by an Act of the legislature itself in 1871, and the educational grant was divided according to population, one half going to the Catholic minority and the other half to the Protestant majority. I have always heard the school question in the province of Manitoba spoken of as the trouble of 1896, but that trouble really developed in 1890, when the legislature passed an Act which annulled the preceding law, and therefore cancelled the enjoyment by the minority of the privileges which they had exercised up to that time with regard to the separate schools.

It was in 1890 that the trouble began. And in my opinion, and in the opinion of those who have been consistent in this line the government of Canada at that time should have refused the Royal assent to this measure of the Manitoba legisla-

ture and, instead of making that law operative, should have sent it back to the legislature of Manitoba. Then, had the province of Manitoba taken the thing up and gone from court to court, the Act of 1871 would have been in force and the separate schools would have remained. After five .or six years of agitation, the Remedial Bill was brought in. But the Bill was not in compliance with the order of the Privy Council. The appeal which was made and which ultimately reached the Privy Council was based on the ground that the Manitoba legislature had refused to provide money for the support of separate schools in that province. The judgment of the Supreme Court was to the effect that money should be provided for the schools of the minority according to the law of the province previous to 1890. That Act was not ultra vires, but it was defective in the sense that it did not give the money necessary for the separate schools, and without such moneys it was impossible to maintain those schools. In the province of New Brunswick during the period of agitation to which I have referred, while we were awaiting the decision of the Privy Council, the minority endeavoured to keep our schools notwithstanding. But after a few months, everybody saw that it would be impossible for the minority to keep their schools on an equality with the public schools which enjoyed grants of public money. And the same thing would have happened in the province of Manitoba. When I say that the Remedial Bill was not in compliance with the order of the Privy Council perhaps I may be allowed to read a few words of that judgment-page 127:

The schools before 1890 received their proportionate share of the money contributed for school purposes out of the general taxation of the province, and the money raised for these purposes by local assessments was, so far as it fell upon Catholics, applied only towards the support of Catholic schools.

What is the position of the Roman Catholic minority under the Act of 1890. Schools of their own denomination, conducted according to their views, will receive no aid from the State. They must depend entirely for their support upon the contribution of the Roman Catholic community, while the taxes out of which the States aid is granted to the schools provided for by 'the Statute fall alike on Catholic and Protestant. Moreover, while the Catholic inhabitants remain liable to local assessments for 'School purposes, the proceeds of that assessment are no longer destined to any extent for the support of Catholic schools, but afford the means of maintaining schools which they regard as
1 more suitable for the eduoation of Catholic children than if they were distinctly Protestant in their character.

This is the basis upon which the judgment of the Privy Council suggested that the government of Canada should provide a Remedial Bill. And what did this Bill provide as it was laid before the House? The first provision was to strike off the appropriation of money for the assistance of schools that the government offered to give the Catholic minority of Manitoba. This Remedial Bill was -opposed by the leader of the opposition ol that time, the hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who leads this opposition to-day. It has been said all over the country that the Remedial Bill should have been accepted by the chief of the opposition, and that in refusing to accept it he had failed to do his duty towards the Catholic people of Manitoba. A great agitation, of which I need not speak further, has been made against him in Quebec and elsewhere. Speaking as a member of the Catholic minority, and as one of the French people, though not of the province of Quebec, I say it was great statesmanship on the part of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to refuse the Bill that was offered. And my reason for saying so is that this Bill did not contain the means necessary for the support of the separate schools. I was a candidate in 1896, and explained my position to the Catholic minority in New Brunswick and to the French Acadians of the county from which I come. I took my stand chiefly upon the very fact that the schools offered by the Remedial Bill were not in a position to be maintained, and for that reason the Remedial Bill of 1896 was not worth the paper it was written on. We had had the experience years before in New Brunswick that schools could not be supported without a share of public money. If the Remedial Bill had been accepted, and if an attempt had been made to put- it into operation in Manitoba, it would have been a great misfortune for the Catholics in that province. For it would have been impossible to maintain their schools upon it, and word would have gone abroad that the Catholic people were not the kind of people to maintain their schools. Is it necessary for me to show the correctness of what I state? I do not believe it is necessary for me to weary the House with reading the provisions of the Bill. But let me say that the Hon. Mr. Dickey in presenting that measure in the House in 1896, declared that the portion which referred to the public money would be eliminated and that that matter would be left in the future, to the good-will of the province. And this notwithstanding the fact that it was on the ground that the province of Manitoba had refused to assist in any way, the schools of the minority

that the agitation, for a Remedial Bill had arisen. We know from speeches delivered in 1896 by members of the then government, between the dissolution of parliament and the elections in June, that they would not give a cent of the public money towards the support of these separate schools, that the supporters of such schools would have to keep them in an efficient state or they would be closed. Therefore, the more this question is considered by any Canadian, no matter from what province he may come, the more thankful he must feel towards Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the settlement which he brought about. It has been said on many occasions that when the history of Canada comes to be written, a black mark will be placed against the name of Laurier because he did not accept that Remedial Bill and thus deprived the Catholic minority in Manitoba of their rights and justice. I believe that when our (history is really written, when impartiality has succeeded to sentiment, it will be proven to the country at large, to Canada, and to the British Empire, that there has been no greater act of statesmanship in the history of Canada than the position taken on that question by Sir Wilfrid Laurier . In view of all these considerations, in view of the agitation which may occur in future, owing to grievances of any part of the population, even although those grievances may not be, and I hope will not be always religious, now while we are forming these new provinces, while we are allotting to them immense territories, with immense possibilities for the future, we should decidedly accept the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John_ (Mr. Pugsley) in order that time may be given for further consideration.

There is one other reason which I wish to give. In to-day's papers I see it stated that the addition of the district of Ungava to the province of Quebec, would not affect the unit of population for the future, that the population of Quebec as at present constituted, would be the pivot of our representation, _ but if correctly reported, Premier Gouin to-day or yesterday stated in the legislature of Quebec that the district of Ungava would be given in the future additional representatives beyond the 65 representatives of the province of Quebec, as it is to-day. I hope he has been misrepresented, but still while there are such rumours I feel that we would he only the more prudent and should insist on adopting the amendment of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in order to give both the government and the members representing the maritime provinces, time to come to some understanding, bearing in mind the possibility of the entrance into the Confederation of Newfoundland, which after all, might be the best strength that could be given to the maritime provinces, Mr. TURGEON.
owing to the harmony of feeling between the people and the similarity in resources.
