358740,ca.proc.d.1912-03-07.1.10.8,1912-03-07,a33ce87d-0860-4816-885e-070b32a2126e,ca.m.7388,Mr. MOLLOY.,,QUESTIONS.,EXTENSION OF BOUNDARIES- MANITOBA.,,Coming as I do from the province of Manitoba and voting as I do against this Bill I think it only fair to my -constituents and to this House that I should explain the reason for my course. This question last came before the House in the closing session of the last parliament on an amendment to the motion for Supply moved by the then member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart). As that was a vote of want of confidence in the government, I voted against the amendment of the then member for Winnipeg and for doing so I received a certain amount of abuse,

I was called a traitor to the province of Manitoba. I was not a traitor to the province of Manitoba. I love Manitoba better than any other province in the confederacy of Canada. I was not born in that province but I was taken there many years ago and my length of residence in Manitoba is greater than that of any other member of this House coming from that province, and anything I may be able to do to assist towards the advancement of Manitoba I would very gladly do.

The boundary question first came into prominence in Manitoba politics in 1905. In that year there was a by-election in the constituency of Mountain owing to the resignation of Mr. Greenway who had been elected to the House of Commons. In that by-election the Conservative candidate was elected by means which could not be defended by everybody. The boundary was made the main issue by the Roblin government. To show its effect in the constituency of Mountain I may say that the gentleman who was elected at the by-election in 1905, against the same Liberal candidate who opposed him in the general election of 1907 the Liberal candidate received the largest majority of any man elected to the legislature in that year. It was again the issue in 1907. I was a candidate in the election of 1907. The Premier of Manitoba said it was a paramount issue. He made many speeches including one notable speech at Carman, on the day of his nomination. He said it was the only issue. With that those of us who were opposed to the Roblin government at that time did not agree.

It was fought out largely on that issue. Mr. Roblin told the people of Manitoba that he would stand by his claim on behalf of his government and that he would not accept anything short of it. He told the people of Manitoba that if any other man than my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had been at the head of affairs in this country Manitoba would have been justly dealt with. I did not believe that then and I do not believe it now. I have felt con-

vinced, ever since this session opened, that two things would happen; in the first place, that Manitoba would not receive such fair treatment from this government as it would have received from the government of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, and second, that the minority in the province of Manitoba would, to use an expression, get tomahawked at the hands of this government. There were some things that were upheld and advocated by Mr. Roblin in the province of Manitoba during the election of 1907. I say that he misled the people of Manitoba with regard to this settlement that he has made. Among other things Mr. Roblin, speaking of the boundary and speaking of the treatment which he was receiving from the then government, said:

I stated at the conference, and I repeat here tonight, that neither Ontario on the one hand nor Saskatchewan on the other have any right either by law or in equity to adjudicate or arbitrate as to what portion of the territory to the north and east Manitoba should have. I say in law, and in making this statement I understand that at once a constitutional question is raised, and I am prepared if Sir Wilfrid Laurier dares undertake to take from us that portion of Kee-watin lying north of Albany river, and which was included in the Act of 1881, and which has not yet been repealed-I say, if Sir Wil-fried Laurier undertakes to deal with that I shall resist it with all the power and all the influence that a united people with a just cause can exercise and command.
A very lofty sentiment.

I will go to the foot of the Throne where justice is always secured and there I believe- I know-that we will get what is ours; we will get what Sir Wilfrid has invited Ontario to claim and which she is ashamed of herself, and thus get at least a portion of the territory he would propose to give to another province.

As a matter of fact, he has not received that territory, and he has not only not received that territory, but he had accepted a great deal less. He has accepted less than that which was offered by the members of the former government in 1908. Speaking at the same meeting he said further on:

We are asking for a territory that Ontario never asked for; no public man in Ontario ever thought of asking for it, because constitutionally they had barred their claim to this particular territory. Sir Wilfrid, however, cunning and designing in his methods of operation to thwart the will of Manitoba invited this province which has no right or interest there to make a claim and they have done so (applause). Now, you say, why cannot you succeed as Sir Oliver Mowat has done? We can and will, if the people of Manitoba stand behind me.
Well, the people of Manitoba supported the Roblin government in 1907, there were

thirteen oppositionists elected. In the general election of 1911, there were thirteen oppositionists elected; so that the people of Manitoba evidently were behind the Premier of that province, and still he has accepted much less than he told the people he would accept. He also said on that same day, speaking with reference to the claims that the province of Saskatchewan was making:

Why do I mention Saskatchewan? I will give you a reason. It is one that will carry conviction to the hearts and consciences of every true Manitoban in this province. WheD we met in conference at Ottawa as I have said, after I had stated my case and after Mr. Whitney had made his pretensions of a claim, knowing he had nothing he could make any argument on, because there was no argument to be made.

That is what Mr. Roblin said in 1907. However, times have changed. The then Minister of Public Works in the Manitoba government is now in Ottawa, and' a member of the present government. He is a strong and influential man-there is no question about that- but he sits beside a man who is also strong and influential, a member of the same Cabinet, and that gentleman is from the province of Ontario. After all the trouble they raised about the boundaries as laid down by the Laurier government in 1908, the hon. Minister off Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) a member of the government of Ontario, made a claim on behalf of that province, and in order to satisfy the wishes of Ontario it was considered necessary by the government to accede to the demands of that hon. gentleman. What is the situation to-day? Here is the old province of Manitoba, here is a portion of the added territory, the northerly portion of which is divided by the Churchill river, and in comes the province of Ontario in the form of a strip five miles wide running from one side of the province of Manitoba to the Nelson river. I wonder what the Premier of Ontario would have said if the government of Manitoba, whether Liberal or Conservative, with the endorsation and assistance of the government of Canada that was in power prior to the 21st of September, had asked the government of Ontario to concede a strip of territory five miles in width Tunning easterly from the Manitoba boundary through the province of Ontario. I wonder what Mr. Whitney would have said, and when Mr. Whitney says * no ' he is given credit for meaning just exactly what he says. But our representatives in the Cabinet, and there are two from Manitoba, have consented to a bargain which is nothing but a jumble on the very face of it. Not only have they given Ontario a roadbed through the province of Manitoba for no reason whatso-

ever, but along with that they have given Ontario some other things as well. In the Ontario legislature the other day members of the opposition found fault with the little that Ontario had received from the bargain that is about to be made. Mr. Hearst in reply said regarding the. strip of territory that is given to Ontario from the Manitoba boundary to the Nelson river:

The Minister of Lands, Forests and Mines, proceeded to point out the advantages Ontario would receive under this arrangement to secure access to Port Nelson. The five-mile strip of the river gave a ten-mile frontage on the south shore and the best shore.
Ten of the best miles on the river will be Ontario's said Mr. Hearst. ' Ten miles frontage on that harbour means that Ontario will own the townsite there if ever it becomes a real harbour.

That statement was received with applause, and no wonder. What I particularly want to point out is that the government of the province of Manitoba would not accept any settlement offered by the Laurier government for the simple reason that it would not pay them politically to do so. They made a football of the Manitoba boundary during the Manitoba campaign on two occasions. They find now that they are about at the end of their tether, and they are willing to act in defiance of the speech made by the now Secretary of State, (Mr. Roche), in 1908, and sitting in the gallery at that time before I had become a membei of this House, I heard that hon. gentleman claim just as Mr. Roblin had done, that under the decision of the Privy Council in 1884, Manitoba was entitled to every foot of that territory known as Keewatin north of the Albany river.

Now, they come back and after all, they accept less from this government than they were, willing to accept from the Laurier government on any consideration. Of course, they had no intention of accepting any terms offered by the Liberal government, because they thought it was good policy-and I regret to say that the result shows it was-t"" hamper the Liberal government in every way and to prevent a settlement so far as they could. However, these things all come to an end, and the Roblin government cannot- work that game much longer. What the Roblin government will do for a policy, now that they are going to get rid of the boundary question, I really do not know.
column2: I am

column1: sure they will not appeal to the country on their telephone policy, or on their Manitoba elevator policy, or on the Manitoba land deals on the part of the Roblin government, or on their administration of justice in Manitoba. Well, perhaps they may go^ to the people on their God-fearing and saintly record as a government for the last twelve or thirteen years. As to the Mr. MOLLOY.

financial terms offered to Manitoba by this Bill, I contend that the province will not be as w'ell off, when the swamp lands are given back to the Dominion, as it was before. The province of Manitoba receives under this legislation, an increase on debt account amounting to $202,637 a year; on land account amounting to $313,270; and the interest on the bulk sum given to the province will amount to $119,013. Along with the boundaries offered by the Laurier government, they were offered by that government a yearly grant of $200,000, and the items I have mentioned above under this present proposal, amount to about $634,000 a year. The $200,000 which would have gone with the boundaries, (plus the strip that Ontario has received), would amount in toto to about $434,000 a year more in cash than was offered by the Liberal government. Now, the statement made by the Hon. Hugh Armstrong, Provincial Treasurer, in Winnipeg last year, will give an idea of what the government of Manitoba valued the swamp lands at. The statement of Mr. Armstrong was made on the 22nd of February, 1910, and is reported in the Winnipeg ' Telegram,' of the 23rd of February, 1910. Accounting for the assets of the province, he made this statement:
Provincial lands, 1,425,712 acres; valued at $3 an acre, and amounting to $4,277,136; swanp lands to be turned over by Dominion government 4,000,000 acres.

It has since been estimated to be more, but we will accept the statement of Mr. Armstrong. At $3 per acre, that would amount to $12,000,000 and plus the one million odd acres sold, it would mean a cash value of $16,000,000 which capitalized at 5 per cent., would amount to $800,000
column2: a year.

column1: condition if they had retained control of the swamp lands. Now, as against that, they receive a cash subsidy of $434,000 a year better than the Laurier government offered. But they give back to the Dominion the swamp lands of the province, which would mean, if capitalized at 5 per cent, $800,000 a year. But, the argument is made that Manitoba will get back the swamp lands. Well, perhaps she will and perhaps she will not. The people of Manitoba have no guarantee that the swamp lands will ever be returned and those who believe that they will not have just as much right for their belief as those who believe to the contrary. My own opinion is that the swamp lands will probably be retained by the Dominion and be administered by the Department of the Interior. Therefore, I say that the financial arrangements as proposed in this Bill are not in the interests of Manitoba. If the swamp lands had remained in the province of course the other terms offered here would be very much to her advant-

age. It was 'but a short time ago that gentlemen opposite were advocating: ' what we have we'll hold.' Let me ask why did not the province of Manitoba retain her swamp lands when she had them? It is my belief that it would be far easier to retain possession of these lands than to ever get them back again. There were over 8,000,000 acres of swamp lands, and at a valuation of $4 an acre they would amount to $32,000,000. According to the statement of the Provincial Treasurer of Manitoba, the lands which were sold were sold at an average price of $5.48 per acre, amounting in all, for the year to $515,298. Last year the statement of the sale of lands alone, outside of subsidies received from other quarters, is as follows:
First payment on land sold.. $ 43,383
Deferred payments
Timber dues, &c
Interest on deferred payments. 166,319

In eight years the province of Manitoba had received from the interest on deferred payments alone, $923,692 and a great part of these were swamp lands. The most damaging feature in connection with the swamp lands is this:
column2: the swamp lands

column1: will now become the property of the Dominion, and as a consequence the drainage will not be done which otherwise would. I call the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the fact that on the fourth of March, 1910, he moved a resolution to the effect that in the opinion of the government of Manitoba it was in the interest of the province that the Dominion should at once turn over to the province the swamp lands so that they could be made into drainage districts. In that way the lands would be drained and they would find more ready sale, and the lands of the settlers adjoining would receive the benefit from the drainage which would have been done. I think that was a very sensible wray to go about it, because when the lands were turned over to the province then not only the swamp lands themselves but the other provincial lands and the lands of the settlers would come under one drainage district and everybody would be benefited. In support of the policy then advocated by the provincial government with respect to swamp lands, I quote no less an authority than the Winnipeg 'Telegram' which 'is the official organ of the Roblin government in Manitoba. On April 5, 1911, the Winnipeg
Telegram ' said in a plainly inspired article:

Under the settlement of the boundary question proposed by Mr. Oliver, 8,000,900 acres of swamp land would likely be transferred to the province. The importance of this assurance contained in Mr. Oliver's communication can hardly be overestimated for it presents the

Dominion government's proposal in an altogether different light. The recent communication from the Dominion government, setting forth the terms under which it would agree to the enlargement of Manitoba's boundaries made no reference to this immense acreage of swamp land which it is proposed to donate to Manitoba, and, the concession of 8,000,000 acres of swamp land is infinitely more important than the cash compensation offered for the surrender of the public domain in the added territory.

It was of infinitely more value than the cash offer of $434,000 better than was offered by the previous government. I may say that the swamp lands were estimated by the late Mr. Young to be 8,232,831 acres at $3 an acre, which, capitalized at 5 per cent, would give an income of $1,234,964. I admit that it would naturally cost the government of Manitoba something to drain that land, and something to put it on the market, but little compared with the value received for it.

We have been told time and again that with the advent to power of the Conservative government the prairie provinces would be given their natural resources. Hon. gentlemen opposite say, we have not had time. There is reason and justice in that statement; but I believe that many moons will pass before the natural resources of the prairie provinces are handed over to them by this government, if it is ever done.

Another question which I want to deal with is the school question, or the rights of the minority of the province of Manitoba and in the territory which is to be added to the province of Manitoba. I listened with great attention to the statements made by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), who is known as a lawyer of high standing in this country, in which statement he tried to justify the action of this government in ignoring those rights. I believe, and I do not care how many authorities are brought forward, that the minority in the province of Manitoba are and have been suffering from a grievance for the last twenty years, and they are determined, and justly so, if it lies in their power, that this shall come to an end. I cast my first vote on the 15th of January, 1896, though I was a Liberal then, as I am a Liberal now, and I voted for the present Conservative member for the county' of Emmerson. My second vote I cast on the 23rd of June, 1896, and I cast it for the gentleman who is now Senator Lariviere from the province of Manitoba. I have been consistent on this question, and I propose to stand out for the rights of those who are suffering from a grievance, and at some time this government or some other government will have to reckon with those people and with their co-religionists throughout this entire coun-

try. I say they have been unfairly treated for political reasons and political reasons only. Just as the Eoblin government made a football of the boundary question for political reasons, so the Liberal government of Manitoba in 1890 made a football of the school question for their own political purposes.

The statement of the Minister of Public Works rather nonplussed me for the time being, when he said that the district of Keewatin did not come under the Act of 1875. I believe that it does come under that Act, for the following reasons:
The district of Keewatin was created as a separate entity by Chap. 21 of the Statutes of Canada, 1876, and by section 9, thereof it was provided that:

All laws in force in the said district as part of the Northwest Territories, at the time of the coming into force of this Act, and not hereby repealed, shall, so far as they are consistent with the ' The British North America Act, 1867/ with the terms and conditions of the admission of Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories into the Union, approved of by the Queen, under the one hundred and forty-sixth section thereof, and with any Aot of the parliament of Canada relating to the Northwest Territories then in force, and with this Act, remain in force in the said district nnfil repealed or altered by the parliament of Canada, or by the Governor in Council, or the Lieutenant Governor and his Council, under this Act, as shall also any Mr. MOLLOY.
order of the Governor in Council made under any Act mentioned in the second seotion of this Act, until repealed, or altered, as it may be, under this Act.

It was also provided that the Governor in Council at any time by a proclamation, should have the right to re-annex the same to the Northwest Territories and when so done, this particular territory should be subject to the same government and laws as that part of the territories to which it was to be re-annexed. This is provided for in the latter portion of section 1, which is as follows:

Provided always that the Governor in Council may, by proclamation published in the ' Canada Gazette/ at any time when it may appear to the public advantage so to do, detach any portion of the said district from the same, and re-annex it to that part of the Northwest Territories not included in the said district; and the portion so detached shall then be subject to the same government and laws as that part of the said territories to which it is re-annexed.

Therefore, at this date clearly the provisions of section 10 of the Educational Act of 1875 were applicable to Keewatin as well as to any or all the other portions of the Northwest Territories. Things remained in this condition until the creation of the new provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, when a new Act was passed regarding the Northwest Territories, known as chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1905, which, while assented to on the 20th of July, 1905 by section 15 of the Act. did not come into force until the last day of September, 1905, and by section 3 of this Act, the Northwest Territories were defined as follows:

The Northwest Territories shall hereafter comprise the territories formerly known as Rupert's Land and the Northwestern Territory, except such portions thereof as form the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the district of Keewatin and the Yukon Territory, together with all British territories and possessions in North America and all islands adjacent to any such territories or .possessions except the colony of Newfoundland and its dependencies.

It will be seen that Keewatin was not included as a portion of the Northwest Territories, but for the time being remained a separate district, but by an order in council passed on the 24th day of July, 1905 under the provisions of section 1 of the statutes of 1876, hereinbefore quoted, it was re-annexed to and became a portion of the Northwest Territories, to take effect on, from and after the first day of September, 1905, which order in council is as follows :-
By proclamation dated 24th July, 1905, under the provisions of the Act, chapter fifty-three of the Revised Statutes of Canada, commonly known as the Keewatin Act, the

whole district of Keewaitin was annexed to that part of the Northwest Territories not included in the said district, on, from and after the first day of September in the year of Our Lord one thousand nine hundred and fire.
It will therefore be seen that on the 1st day of September, Keewatin became a portion of the Northwest Territories.

We do not hesitate to declare that every Catholio of French tongue, anxious for our school rights, is in honour hound to support his candidate.
Commenting upon the result of the general election of October 26, 1908, ' Les Cloches ' made the following remarks, and they have lost nothing of their aptness and their justice:-
' The result of this election has been a majority of about 50 for the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
' The county of Provencher has elected a Liberal and an Irish Catholic.
' The French-Canadians who did not vote for the Hon. Mr. La riviere have forgotten the Mr. MOLLOY.

pact made upon the organization of the electoral divisions here which assured to the French-Canadians the election of one of their own race. They have forgotten, also, that it was the Liberal government which in 1890 abolished the official use of the French language. Catholics who voted for Mr. Lari-viere forgot that it was the Liberal Greenway government which took from us our schools in 1890, that it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier, head of the Liberal party at Ottawa, who opposed, in 1896, the Remedial Bill, establishing the principles of separate schools and presented to the House by the Grand Orange Master, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, that it was the same Sir Wilfrid Laurier who in 1905 did not have the courage to concede all our school-rights, especially the right of the confessional school, guaranteed by the constitution, in Saskatchewan and Alberta, that the so-called final Laurier-Greenway settlement of 1896 gives us none of out former school-rights from the Catholio standpoint, although it gives us a portion of our rights to the French language, placing us, however-us, the first occupants of this country-on the same footing as all other settlers speaking a language other than English. These are incontestable facts, whicli one may try to weaken or explain, but which remain absolutely true and which many know without appearing to be at all disturbed.

' There is no doubt that in the present contest the county of Provencher will he able to recover itself and to regain the position lost in 1908. This county belongs by right to the French-Canadians and to the French Metis, who form the majority and who must inwardly desire to he represented by one of their own race and not by a man who is a stranger to their nationality, and to their language. May the regard for superior interests and for patriotism win the day over the blind party spirit, and may all the French-speaking electors in the county of Provencher contribute by their votes to assure themselves a Catholic and French-Speaking member.'

I am sure that will satisfy anybody as to the direction in which it was thought advisable that the Catholic vote should go in the province of Manitoba, and especially in the constituency of Provencher. Now, we shall see whether they will receive more from the gentlemen who are in power here, and from those who have been kept in power in Manitoba for the last ten or twelve years by this same vote. This is not a political question-or should not be. I am going to support the man and the measure which will give to the minority in Manitoba that to which they are entitled-and they are asking nothing .more-as guaranteed them by the constitution. And if it has come to this, that a religious body, in order to receive justice, must be in the majority, there is something wrong with the existing state of things. In Manitoba the separate schools were taken away,-and let them say of those schools what they will; there was no need to abolish the separate school system in Manitoba; if that system was not

right, it could be reformed. And I say I will give my support only to that man and that measure, which will restore to the Catholics of Manitoba and the territory to be annexed to Manitoba, the rights which they formerly enjoyed. And beyond any question of doubt, the Catholics have a greater right to separate schools in this added territory even than in the old province of Manitoba. I hope the government will see their way clear to secure for these people the rights to which they are entitled as clearly as the Catholics of Ontario are entitled to the rights which nobody would deny them, as are -also the Protestants of Quebec. I remember hearing the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) state in his first speech this session, that it was no disgrace to a man to have gone down with the good cause in 1896. If it was a good cause in 1896, it is a better cause to-day. On behalf of the Catholics of Manitoba being the only Catholic in parliament, from that province, I claim for them these rights to which they are entitled. And the day will come when their rights will be given to them, whether the government of that day be Conservative or Liberal. And we will thank nobody for it, because we are asking only for that to which we are entitled.

BONIFACE SOUNDS THE TOCSIN.,,It is neither my purpose nor my desire to take up the time of the House at great length. But this Bill is of such far reaching consequence, that I think it my duty as representing a constituency of eastern Canada to offer some observations with respect to it. While -the title of the Bill is: ' An Act to provide for the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba,' the Bill is not confined either in its provisions or in its consequences, to one particular province. It is so far-reaching that it certainly affects every province in eastern Canada.

Shortly after Confederation, in 1868, as a land speculation if you will, the Dominion purchased what were known as the Hudson bay lands, a venture which was conceived to be in the interests of the provinces. It is now conceded on all hands that it was a wise speculation, not only in the interests -of the original provinces, but in the interests of the great country that was purchased by the Canadian Confederation. And from_ that day down to the present, every province of the Dominion has been interested in our western heritage, as it has been called.

Every province in the Dominion has looked to that western country with pride, with a feeling of proprietary right, and not merely with respect to the good which was to come to the eastern provinces, but with respect to the good which was to come to the country carved out as our Northwest Territories. The original

partners were Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario and when British Columbia and Prince Edward Island came into the partnership they entered having equal rights with the original provinces, and were entitled to share with the original provinces all the benefits that might accrue, and they assumed their proportion of the responsibilities, which were placed upon the Confederation by the act of absorption of these western territories. It is not merely the question of the investment of the original purchase money, not merely the dollars and cents involved in the securing of the western country but from the moment of the purchase down to the present each of the eastern provinces has given of its best to the upbuilding of our great western territory, to the creation of a great west that would invite the millions from all lands. To the upbuilding of the western country the eastern provinces have contributed of their brain and their brawn, year after year we have poured into the west our young men, our. very best, with a view not merely of upbuilding that country but of advancing the individual interests of those who thought it desirable to make their homes in the western land. In the face of great difficulties we have built up a confederacy which has attracted to us the eyes of Europe, the eyes of Great Britain, the eyes of the people to the south of us. Chief among the difficulties that presented themselves to those who were charged with the duty of- creating the federation was the question of finances. Had not some assurance been given particularly to the peoplfc of (the Maritime provinces that financial arrangements would be made sufficient to guarantee them from any direct taxation in order to carry on the government of their respective provinces, there would have been no confederacy. When Sir John Macdonald, the Hon. Geo. Brown and their associates went to Charlottown, at a time when the delegates of the several maritime provinces were meeting to consider the question of a maritime union and presented their proposition with respect to a larger and wider confederation, one of the very first questions asked of them by the men of the maritime provinces was: Upon what terms can such an arrangement be entered into with respect to the financial future of our provinces. At that time each province had entire control of its excise and customs duties and of all revenues, and they wished to know how they could receive compensation for surrendering these revenues and how they could carry on the affairs of their local administration. The second question was with respect to the binding of these provinces together. The provinces were then aliens and strangers to each other.

not settled right, and it is not settled for the further reason that it leaves all these matters open to future adjustment. Instead of calling this ' An Act to provide for the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba.' I would call it ' An Act to create entanglements and embarrassments as respects our western heritage and to make confusion for all time to come in the matter of provincial subsidies.' That, in my judgment, is the proper appellation for the Bill now before the committee. It is calculated to create entanglement and embarrassment as respects our western country. You tentatively have arranged boundaries for Manitoba and you have carved out of if an area for Ontario, thus placing across the territory of Manitoba a bar sinister, and affording a pathway which is calculated to create disturbance, to cause confusion and to engender irritation between those two great provinces. You have (provided in your Bill conditions for the creation of jealousies among the other provinces of the Dominion.

In the public prints of to-day we observe that the province of Saskatchewan has put in its claims. This is a question which, like Banquo's ghost, will never down, which will always be before the Canadian people. This government may not live very long to grapple with it; but succeeding governments will be confronted with the same difficulties. This matter is not settled, and cannot be settled, until it is grappled with, with a courage that has not been evinced by this government. With respect to [DOT] the provincial subsidies, the original basis has been departed from, from time to time. In f906, I think it was, the right hon. leader of the opposition, then the leader of the government of Canada, invited the representatives of the several provinces to take into consideration the question of subsidies. We know the history of that conference, and we realize the position that was taken by the Premier of British Columbia. That gentleman refused to be reconciled, refused even to consider the judgment of his colleagues in the conference, and went away; and that question has been in British Columbia, from that time down to the present, and I doubt not will be for years to come, a disturbing element, a matter upon which provincial elections will be run, and which may become an issue in any Dominion election that may be contested in that province, either a general or a by-election. To the detriment of other great questions, it will cause injury not only 'to the province, but to the Dominion at large. If our human ideals were attained, we would, have great issues settled by the people of the several provinces upon their merits; but when you leave as matters of contention, issues that are local, you have those Mr. KMMERSON.

issues engrossing the minds of the electors to the exclusion of greater issues that affect the Dominion at large. Therefore, I say that in this regard this Bill will not only create confusion, but is a menace to the future of this Dominion, a menace to the good government of Canada, a menace to the parliament of Canada in its consideration of the great iquestions entrusted to it for solution. From that standpoint I condemn this Bill, and I say that it does not meet the difficulties, that it does not attempt to grapple with and solve the difficulties, that it is imperfect, incomplete, and as such deserves the condemnation, not only of this House, but of the people of Canada at large. Who wants simply to half settle a matter? There must be in the mind of every man here, I care not what his political faith may be, a desire to see all these difficulties, as between the federal government and the provincial governments respectively, settled and determined, so that they can be brushed from our pathway, and we can follow along the road of national government in the interest of the whole people, and without regard to any merely sectional prejudice or passion.

Another thing. This question, however settled, affects the future representation in this House of Commons, and as such dbes an injury to eastern Canada. As such it affects the little province of Prince Edward Island very materially. That province has contributed to the upbuilding of the western country, with its brain and its brawn, with young men and young women going from its shores every season. That little province is being depleted-shall I say impoverished? No, because it is so rich and fertile that it is almost impossible to impoverish the ' Garden of the Gulf.' But it is being injured, and1 its representation in this House is decreasing year by year until we can in vision see that it has reached almost the vanishing point. If we go on in the same ratio, the time will come when the constituency of Prince Edward Island will be joined to that of Westmorland, and we shall have an electoral district composed of the county of Westmorland in New Brunswick, with Prince diward Island thrown in and sending one member to this House. The next distribution, I understand, will give Prince Edward Island three members, while it has four senators in the Senate of Canada. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), spoke, I am sure with sincerity, and with a desire to accomplish the very best possible for the province which he so ably represents in this government. But my hon. friend has been too long in politics to be in any way caught by fair promises, and I an! that he must realize that now is the time to have this whole problemTsolved. When

we are discussing the financial arrangements with Manitoba, when we are taking into consideration the enlargement of Ontario, when we are contemplating a solution of the difficulties in the prairie provinces, and when we have in mind the coming to Ottawa of the Premier of British Columbia with his claims, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries must realize, if he realizes anything that now is the time to strike, while the iron is hot, that now is the time to demand for his province, and the other provinces by the sea, the consideration which they should have.

My hon. friend said that the case of Manitoba was urgent. What greater urgency could there be than in the case of the province of New Brunswick, or than in the case of the province of Nova Scotia? There it is assuredly a question of urgency, it is a question which I might almost say is essential to the future of these provinces by the sea. The Minister of Marine is aware that to-day the province of New Brunswick is awaking [DOT]With respect to its future, that its people are alive to the' conditions that confront them, that their environments have created an unrest that is in evidence today in that province. I have in my hand a badge to be worn by delegates from the whole of the province of New Brunswick to a convention that to-morrow is to be held in the city of Fredericton, a convention to take into consideration the conditions -which prevail in that province with respect to the depletion of its population.

Scotia. We cannot get the land itself, although we are not without a precedent forgetting it. I submit to the Prime Minister with confidence that unless he is going to the imperial parliament for confirmatory legislation, he has no constitutional authority for the Bill now before the House. Inasmuch as the province is not in debt, the said province shall be entitled to be paid and to receive from the government of Canada by half-yearly payments in advance, interest at the rate of five per cent per annum on the sum of $422,900.
Will any person in this House deny that that section is a part of the constitution of Manitoba? Then when you come to section 4 of this Bill, it commences:

Inasmuch as the province was not in debt at the time it was established, &c., and you are practically to all intents and purposes repealing section 2 of the Manitoba Aot and putting in its stead sections 4 and 5 of this Bill. My contention is that even if the constitution of a province came only from this parliament, we could not afterwards change it, but how much more is that the case w'hen we find that the charter of Manitoba is practically an imperial Act. At page 2927 of ' Hansard ', 1905, appears an opinion given by Mr. Borden, now Prime Minister, upon the authority of this parliament to tinker with or change the constitution of a province once it is given. The right hon. gentleman then said:

I do not know whether my hon. friend is quite of the same opinion to-day, with regard to the easy nature of the step, but I venture to say in all seriousness that the step which we are taking now is the most important and momentous step that has ever been taken

by this parliament in regard to our Northwestern Territory. We are doing to-day what this parliament cannot undo in the future, because the constitution whioh we now propose to give to the territories of the Northwest can only be adhered by the imperial parliament.

The Prime Minister then took the ground that once a constitution was given to a province nothing could be done by this parliament that would interfere with it. I think that I can successfully contend before any authoritative body on constitutional law, that the Bill now before parliament has the effect of changing the constitution of the province of Manitoba and that we are attempting to legislate in this direction without any authority under our constitution.

them, they wish to leave them as they are, and the old slogan of last summer, let well enough alone, is brought into piay again. Everything within those boundaries will constitute the one province. There will be no north, south, east or west about it, all that territory will be in the province of Manitoba. When Sir John A. Macdonald and his government drafted section 22 of the Manitoba Act, will anybody tell me that it was not his intention to give separate schools in that part of Manitoba. The section provides:
In and for the province, the said legislature, may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions:
Nothing in any such la.w shall prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to Denominational schools which any class of persons have by law or practice in the province at the Union.

It was the intention of the government of that day to give separate schools to the people of Manitoba. It was the belief of the people who went into Manitoba that under that law they had that right. When that section came to be interpreted by the

Lords of the Privy Council they said: There is no doubt about it, that was the intention of that legislation, but the drafters of the Act did not use apt language to fully carry out what they set out to do. Now the Prime Minister, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and every other lawyer in the cabinet, and every man that is in the cabinet or is supporting it, cannot escape the responsibility by saying that there is nothing in the Territories Act to enable them to change the law. All they have to do now when if they are giving a new charter, or a new constitution, to Manitoba and I challenge anybody on the other side to say to the contrary-that if they are giving a new constitution to Manitoba changing its financial terms, and changing its boundaries, what is the matter, if they are true to their principles, with changing that section to give what it was intended to give from the start. That is the condition, Sir, and there is no use in hon. gentlemen trying to escape by any back door, or by saying there is nothing in the Territories Act which gives them the right to do this. If the government had the right to change the financial terms, they have the right to change other features. They cannot escape their responsibility and they may as well confess that they do not want to do it. That is the position and that is where I want to leave it. Now I submit that all these things should be put right, and that the province should get what belongs to it. If these matters are not righted now there will be an appeal to Caesar, there will be an appeal to the people. If we cannot get our rights here, we will get them at the ballot-box, and this government will be hurled from power and will have plenty of time to lament not taking the action which they could have taken in this matter.

BONIFACE SOUNDS THE TOCSIN.,,The Bill before the House is, in my judgment, one of the most important measures that has ever been introduced in parliament since [DOT]confederation. As has been pointed out by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, it is in effect, an attempt at recasting the terms of confederation. It goes to the very essence of our constitution, It deals with matters that pertain to all the provinces, and with especially matters of very vital importance to each and every one namely, the extent of its territory and the financial arrangements under which it came into confederation, and form part and parcel of that grand scheme. I shall say nothing as to the rights of the people in the addition which is being made under this Bill to the province of Manitoba. I want to deal more particularly with this special point:
column2: I represent a constituency which, from what I

column1: have heard within the last few days, regarding the effect of the late census on the question of representation, will stand a good chance of being wiped out. I am quite convinced, after listening to the eloquent speech of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries yesterday, that it was not the intention of the fathers of confederation that any of the maritime provinces should lose the representation which they had at that time. I have the honour to speak for a constituency that was represented about the time of the union and afterwards by men who took a prominent part in the confederation scheme and afterwards in the securing of better terms. I refer to one of the bright and shining lights of confed-ration one who took a prominent part in the confederation deliberations, William A. Henry, subsequently, Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, who at that time, represented the county to which 1 have the honour to belong. I refer likewise, to the late judge Hugh Macdonald, who also represented the county of Anti-gonish, and who after confederation went to England to secure better terms for his native province. I am quite sure that if these men could have anticipated that the county of Antigonish would- be put into the position it is likely to be, by reason of the legislation which is now before the House, and legislation which will be brought down with respect to the extension of the boundaries of Quebec-not directly due to that legislation, but indirectly due to it-I am quite sure that if they could have foreseen that the constitution would be construed in the way that it is likely to be construed, they would have taken care that more apt language was used in connection with the clauses dealing with the question of representation, than was used. It has been pointed out by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who backed up the members from this side of the house that the provinces by the sea, are likely to be placed in a very humiliating position by reason of the great growth that is going on in the western part of the country, due in a large measure to the drain that has been made upon the eastern provinces. They are likely to have their representation still further reduced. I have listened with a great deal of pleasure and satisfaction to that hon. gentleman's statement when he said that we should approach this question without any party spirit. On this question, he said, .all those from the maritime provinces, should be united. I agree that, it is a most serious question, and I invite hon. gentlemen opposite, and especially those from the maritime provinces, to show that they appreciate the gravity of the situation by urging upon the government to afford some protection to that section of Canada before this measure Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonis'.i.

goes through. Now is the time, I submit to do that, when the province of Manitoba is asking for an extension of her boundaries and for a change in the terms and conditions under which it entered confederation, and under which it existed in that confederation for a period of 40 years%

The province of Quebec, as explained by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is to have almost an empire added to it. And the papers tell us that the province of Saskatchewan is asking for further consideration and for redress of grievances which it alleges will exist if this measure goes through. Does anybody doubt for a moment that, if we give this large territory to Manitoba and make the proposed subventions to that province, the other provinces will be discontented? Though I have listened to this debate carefully I havj not heard a solitary, substantia! reason advanced in supnort of these concessions to Manitoba, except that Manitoba is a young, energetic, active province that was well worthy of the advantages proposed to be given, and deserving to be as well treated as Alberta and Saskatchewan. There was no constitutional ground for the favours to be granted-only a comparison with Alberta and Saskatchewan. We are asked to depart from the terms of confederation on which Manitoba came in and under which she has existed since, and this is to be done on the plea that it is necessary in order to place Manitoba on, an equal footing with Alberta and Saskatchewan-not because there are constitutional grounds for the change. But what about the other provinces of the Dominion? What about New Brunswick? What about Prince Edward Island? Have not these provinces equal rights with Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba? And if you are going to make an increased grant to Manitoba simply because a certain grant was made to Alberta and Saskatchewan and not because there is a legal constitutional ground for it, why not deal in the same way with the maritime provinces and British Columbia?

This is the time when the people of the maritime provinces should urge their grievance. That there is a grievance, no one can deny who has listened to the calm and earnest speech of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) and to the speeches of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) and the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Em-merson). Anybody who listened to these speeches, whether in sympathy with the maritime provinces or not, if he applies reason, judgment and fair-play to the question must come to the conclusion that the people of the maritime provinces have a just and valid claim, that they have a

grievance that should be redressed. I refer to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the speech he delivered to show that in my judgment we should look at this question not from the party point of view. We should not seek to make party capital out of it.

It was pointed out by the hon. member for Westmorland that the intention of the fathers of confederation was that the maritime provinces should continue to have the representation that they had on entering confederation. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries emphasized that. But the whole difficulty is that the intention was not expressed; what was intended to be said was not said, or that which was said was different from that which was intended. But that is not by any means unprecedented. The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) referred to the Manitoba school case and to the decision of the Privy Council, showing conclusively from the language of the members of that court that there was no doubt as to what was intended so far as Manitoba was concerned, which was separate schools, but the difficulty was that apt language was not used, and they had to consider the language used and give their decision accordingly. It was pointed out by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and others that the idea of the fathers of confederation was that the representation of the maritime provinces should bear a certain proportion to that of the rest of Canada. But what was meant by Canada? The maritime provinces contended that it meant the original four provinces. But the courts held that it meant the Dominion of Canada as it then was, including the added provinces. And we suffer in consequence, and we must accept the constitution as it is. But we appeal to this government to take steps to secure for the maritime provinces that which it was originally intended they should have. I say it is time that we should press our claims, now when other provinces are coming and asking that justice be done. When the half of Canada is asking for changes, seeking favours and concessions-justice if you like-from this parliament, that is the time when we should be more likely to get the ear of this parliament and of the other provinces for our own demand. The Prime Minister intimated yesterday that something would be done for the maritime provinces. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries also gave us some comfort in that regard. But the statements of the Prime Minister were rather vague and indefinite and, while in form reassuring and comforting, were far from satisfactory. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who was rather more assuming so far as the rights of the maritime provinces are concerned, asked us not to throw

any obstacle in the way of this measure, not to press our claim just now, but to take the chance of the goodwill and generosity of the other provinces at a later date. I concur in what the hon. member from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) said, that the time when others are seeking for redress of grievances, the time when the other party is seeking a favour from you, is the proper time to do business. The words of the Prime Minister were somewhat comforting and the words of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries perhaps were well conceived. Yet I think the words of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) were far from comforting. The Prime Minister tells us that later on the provinces by the sea would be taken into his council and he would see wrhat could be done for them. But he did not promise definitely that anything would be done. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries went further and said he hoped the day was not far distant when these grievances would be settled and thus justice done.

The Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works rather ridiculed the claim that we made. The latter was somewhat sarcastic when discussing our claims. Tlhe argument of the imaritime provinces is that this large territory which is to be added to the province of Manitoba is not the patrimony of Manitoba but the equal property of all the rest of Canada. It was purchased by the four original provinces, costing $1,500,000, but since then there has been expended on it a vast sum of money for surveys, policing and development, the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific and other railways, and it is surely right for the other provinces to say that we must jealously guard our own interests with respect to ""that country. The Minister of Public Works grew sarcastic and ridiculed this claim. He said:

When we heard the hoti. member speak of the necessity, in the disposal of these great territories, of consulting provinces far removed from the regions which we are discussing, and talking of compensation being given to these provinces, one would suppose we were assisting a land deal. Well, that is not the split in which the founders of confederation proceeded; that is not the spirit which presided over the negotiations when they acquired Rupert's Land and the territories of the northwest. There was no payment there for real estate; it was under an order in council of the imperial government that most of these lands were handed over to us, and, while it is true, that in 1868, compensation was paid to extinguish the rights-other than trading and commercial rights of the Hudson's Bay Company, the idea at the bottom of it was that these territories would afterwiards

be distributed among the provinces in order to complete a symmetrical plan under which this territory would become provinciality organized for the fuller and more completed development of the confederacy than in an embryo state. It is not a matter of adjusting accounts among the provinces; it is not a matter to be taken up in a book-keeping spirit; but it is a matter which should he regarded in the light alone of the fruition of the scheme of confederation. It seems to me, therefore, that the criticism we have heard to-day about the financial terms granted and about consulting the other provinces and about an accord between Manitoba and Ontario, as to a right of way for a purely provincial railway into the hinterland and towards Hudson bay; it seems to me that the constitutional points raised in these questions did not evince on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite that large and liberal-minded view which we should take of an event of this kind.

It may be that the Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General, who spoke on similar lines, think that this is a matter of no great importance or concern to us, and that we should look at it in a big, broad, liberal-minded way. That is not the way the people of the maritime provinces look at it, Conservatives as well as Liberals. They feel that all the provinces must have a fair proportionate share of this land in order to carry on their administration. As the hon. member tor North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) pointed out. when Louisiana was purchased by the United States, a large tract of the land was reserved and afterwards dealt out to the various states of the Union. The states received large grants for the support of colleges devoted to agriculture and the mechanical arts. This was done under the Morel College Land Act which was approved on July 2, 1862. We in the maritime provinces are far removed from that western country, but we have a right to participate, and some scheme could be worked out similar to the Morel Act. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have urged that the further consideration of the rights of the maritime provinces should be deferred until this matter is disposed of. I venture to say that if that is done then later on, when the maritime provinces ask to have their case dealt with, they will be told that they should have presented their claim in 1912, when there was a readjustment of the boundaries of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba, and of the indemnity paid to Manitoba. I submit that the time for us to present our case is now, and that there is nothing unreasonable in asking the government to let this matter stand over until a conference of the various Premiers may be held on the question of fair and equitable readjustment of the subsidies. The Mr. CHISHOLM (AntigonisJP

principle of the extension of the Manitoba boundary has already been recognized by the seconding of the Bill. The people of Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec wil'l not suffer from the postponement, and I submit that if this measure goes through it will practically for ever bar the maritime provinces from coming in and securing a redress of grievances. It is now or never with us.

If that be the case, I think it is only fair that the further consideration of this matter should stand over until this question of what our rights in the maritime provinces, both as to representation and provincial subsidies has been determined. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries pointed out that we would likely have our grievances redressed a little later on. The language of the Minister of Marine was somewhat assuring, but the language of the Prime Minister was rather less assuring, while the language of the Minister of Public Works and of the Postmaster General, in referring to the claims of the maritime provinces, was positively disheartening. How far did the Prime Minister go in this connection? He said:

And I would like to repeat what I have already said in speaking upon the resolutions in that regard, that when we do come to consider -that proposal I think- it will -be just and necessary to give some consideration to the maritime provinces whose -boundaries cannot be enlarged by reason of their natural situation, to call them into our councils and give them a just voice as -to the terms upon which these lands shall be handed over, and especially with regard to what compensation, if any, should be given to the three maritime provinces by reason of the transfer of these lands to the governments of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan.

It will be observed that the Prime Minister was very -careful not to commit himself to the statement that the maritime provinces reasonably could expect to participate in these lands at a later day. He said that they would -consider what compensation, if any, might be granted, and he said that they would be called to the councils of the government, but nothing further than that. That surely -cannot be satisfactory to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who come from the maritime provinces. They may have some further assurance that we know nothing of. If they have I can understand the position that they will take hut, if they have iiot any assurance further than these words in the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister, speaking in the debate, they are recreant to their duty to the maritime provinces if they do not take a firmer and more positive stand on this occasion. This is the time for us to act and to act unitedly if we hope to accomplish anything. The hon. Minister of the Interior emphasized

the fact last night that the people of Manitoba have had a long standing grievance, that they had been complaining in season and out of season ever since they had entered confederation, and in order to placate them it was necessary to come down with some such measure as this. He emphasized the fact that they had complained, that they had remonstrated with this government time and time again ever since confederation. They succeeded, or they are about to succeed. Therefore, I say it is up to the people of the maritime provinces, who have been suffering in patience, who have been quietly seeing their population dwindle away census after the census, who find that the finances of the various provinces are scarcely sufficient to carry on their business in a satisfactory manner, and who are handicapped very much because of their limited revenue, to get busy now and try and secure from this government the measure of compensation that they are entitled to. They should take a leaf out of the book of Manitoba. They should agitate, they should remonstrate with the Prime Minister, who, we are proud to acknowledge, is one of our own people from the maritime provinces and whose sympathies are, or should, naturally be with us. It is up to the people of the maritime provinces to make their grievances known and to press their grievances in season and out of season, so that they may secure that measure of justice to which they are entitled.

Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.) There is no doubt that the province of Prince Edward Island is presenting to the government certain claims which they expect to be considered and which are really at the *present time under consideration,. The government of the province of Manitoba is also presenting claims which, we understand, are to be settled by arbitration. If this Bill passes there is no doubt but that other claims will be presented by nearly all the provinces because this Biil will unsettle the financial arrangements between the federal government and the provincial administrations.

Would it not be a just thing to do, to accept the amendment of the hon. member for St John (Mr. Pugsley) and call together all the provinces to present all their claims so that the Dominion government may dispose of them at one and the same timejl If you adopt this Bill you will practically issue an invitation to all the provincial governments to come here and present the claims they have or think they have, and then you will be compelled to dispose of these claims in a fragmentary way. Prince Edward Island thinks it is entitled to consideration because of the public domain that is being given to the other provinces, and it appears to me this government has some idea that there is merit in that claim because the Prime Minister, speaking on the subject, gave us an intimation that when the three prairie provinces are given the ownership of their lands the government would consider the claims of the maritime provinces for compensation in reference thereto. I fear it will be many years before that matter is disposed of, and if Prince Edward Island has to wait that long for compensation, it is certain the subsidy to that province will not be increased in the near future. I would, however, point out to the Prime Minister, that although he himself gave that promise, and although it was concurred in to some extent by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, no other member of his government who spoke appeared to take the same view. The remarks of the Minister of Labour would lead us to suppose that he did not think there was anything in the claim of the maritime provinces with regard to this; the Minister of Finance appeared to take the same ground, but the Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) strongly disapproved of the idea that the maritime provinces, had any claim in regard to the public domain that would be handed over to the other provinces, and the Minister of Public Works indeed said that the hinterland of Quebec and Ontario had always belonged to these provinces and that it was always understood it would be handed over to them in due time. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) told us that we should not approach this question in any huckstering spirit, but in a broad and generous way, and judging by his attitude, it would seem to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) would be quite pleased to take the land for Quebec and to leave the broad and generous spirit to the maritime provinces. Surely there can be no better time to settle this whole matter than the present. It is a matter that concerns us in the maritime provinces very intimately.
When this matter was first discussed the member for Kings and Albert (Mr Fow-Mr HUGHES (Kings).

ler) made the statement that this measure would not pass until the maritime provinces got fair-play and justice, and the hon. memebr for Queens, Prince Edward Island, agreed with him in that view. These gentlemen are not here to-night but if they were I have no doubt they would be just as insistent as we upon this side of the House are in seeing that we get a more definite statement in regard to this question. I have presented my views on the matter, I think they are fair and reasonable views, and I believe they should receive just consideration from the government. We do not want to retard this legislation; we do not want to be unfair to Manitoba or to any province in the Dominion, but we want to get fair-play for the maritime provinces.

Mr. Armstrong also stated that the province was at that time receiving a revenue from the school lands, cash, and deferred payments, of $166,056. I think that this must necessarily be taken into consideration in dealing with the question as to whether this proposed settlement is fair or unfair to the other provinces and particularly to

the smaller provinces of Canada. In my opinion, instead of passing this Bill as it is, instead of going through this farcical arrangement of taking back from the province of Manitoba its swamp lands, with the idea that two or three or four or five years from now they will be handed back, in connection with some arrangement with the three prairie provinces, it would be infinitely better, in view of the fact that the Dominion to-day is administering for the province two sections in every township, or one-seventeenth of the entire area of the lands of Manitoba, to let the province keep her swamp lands, keep as she will under this Bill the school lands, keep the lands in the added territory if you like, and give her a fair and reasonable, nay, a liberal sum, to enable her properly to administer affairs in the added territory. The proposal as it affects subsection 2 of section 4 arises as to the debt allowance. It would almost seem unnecessary at this stage of the debate to approach the question of debt allowance from an historical point of view. Yet it is necessary to make some reference to it in order that one may place before the House a connected statement in regard to the matter. From what I have *been able to gather myself, and from what I have gathered from the remarks of hon. gentlemen on both sides, I have come to the conclusion that the whole question of debt allowance is more or less of a fiction. The payment of the debt allowance itself is a fact but founded upon fiction. In the year of confederation, or the year prior to that event, when negotiations took place, and when the agreement was made between the representatives of the various provinces, the question of debt was a most difficult one to handle.
In old Canada, or in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, large sums

had been expended on public works. We had not paid the money, we owed the money. New Brunswick had a debt, and Nova Scotia had a debt, and after many conferences and much discussion the founders of confederation finally reached an agreement that the debt of Canada, or of ""Ontario and Quebec should be assumed by the Dominion. At first it was stated at $67,000,000, but latterly at $62,000,000, that of New Brunswick at $7,000,000, and that of Nova Scotia at $8,000,000. Now the peculiarity of that assumption of debt was this: The provinces were relieved of their obligations and of their payment of interest. From thenceforth the Dominion of Canada was to bear the obligation and to pay the interest.

We transferred our assets to the Dominion of Canada, we made nothing out of the transaction at all; the Dominion of Canada assumed the debt and took over the assets, themselves. Now, under conditions such as I have narrated, why should a new' province entering confederation without debt have a debt allowance at all. That, I submit, is the fiction in connection with the whole matter. I do not believe there ever should have been a debt allowance to provinces which came into confederation without actually having a debt. But the custom has been followed, in ail cases since confederation to make a debt allowance when any new province did enter confederation, so that it is probably too late at this present time to raise such an objection. But T am convinced in my own mind the whole theory of debt allowance is wrong, the whole thing is founded in fiction and should not have been allowed in the first instance. But we have done otherwise, and having done otherwise in regard to all the other provinces, I do not think we should make an exception in regard to the province of Manitoba. As each province entered into confederation a dtebt allowance was fixed. ' The amount was settled by agreement between the parties interested, and once having been fixed, settled, and adjusted, it should, I think, have been the proper course to have pursued that the settlement made should have remained final and unalterable. But I must admit that it has not in the case of various provinces had that finality. The debt allowance of the various provinces has been on more than one occasion revised, and on more than one occasion altered, but the principle has been adhered to as nearly as possible. The original principle upon which the provinces entered into confederation under actual agreement should1 be adhered to as nearly as may be, particularly where any change might work to the prejudice of one of our sister provinces.

I know he will realize that in handling the money of the people of Canada he is handling trust money and that as in his career up to the present time in the city of Toronto he has handled very large amounts of trust money, I believe that if the case is fairly presented to him it will appeal to him that, as the trustee for the people of Canada, as the trustee of the money in the public treasury, he must have a much stronger case than has been made out here to authorize him to take $2,000,000 odd out of the treasury and hand it over to Manitoba when that money belongs to the people of Canada and when forty per cent of it has been paid in taxes by the people of Ontario. I think that if the case is fairly presented to him he will be impressed with the responsibility which he must carry with regard to this transaction. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) has discussed this question and he is in his place tonight. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), I believe, was prepared to swallow the whole thing in one gulp, but even he had to say that it was an awkward point which had been raised in regard to these arrears and that there was ground for argument. BONIFACE SOUNDS THE TOCSIN.,,Does the hon. member understand that there was no principle of equality when Alberta and Saskatchewan were constituted provinces? Did the measure proposed by the late administration which he supported establish a basis of inequality as between Alberta and Saskatchewan? The hon. member contrasts the population of Manitoba with that of Saskatchewan, but why does he not contrast the population of Manitoba with that of Alberta, or the population of Saskatchewan with the population of Alberta? In order to make a ooint against the measure we have in hand, the hon. gentleman is driven to conclusions which would point directly against the measure he supported in 1905. He asks us to name the principle upon which we make this debt allowance, after he has himself declared that the debt allowance to Alberta and Saskatchewan was based on no principle at all. But, I have a very good answer to his question and it is that we base the debt allowance in this case upon the principle that the province of Manitoba is entitled to be placed on an equality with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I have already conceded that in the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan it was only an expedient for enabling these provinces to proceed with their national housekeeping
and to take care of their public expenditure.

Then the hon. gentleman asked why in the name of all that is sensible any land allowance should be made to Manitoba especially during the past three or four years when Manitoba has not had these lands. The hon. gentleman has argued this whole question more or less as if he were arguing a lawsuit, and I would remind him of the well known principle: that equity regards that as having been done which ought to have been done; and inasmuch as the province of Manitoba should have and would have had these her boundaries extended in 1908, if the financial terms now accorded had been granted to that province at that time, I say it is no more than just that we should compensate Manitoba now. The hon. gentleman seems to overlook the fact that according to the measure he himself supported in 1885 without a murmur, the compensation in lieu of lands was based on population, and I would ask him why it is that a very large allowance in lieu of public lands should be made to Alberta and Saskatchewan and only a trifling allowance in comparison should be made to Manitoba. Inasmuch as these three provinces have not their own natural resources, inasmuch as these resources within their boundaries are administered by the government of Canada, we are disposed to regard them all as in the same category, and for that reason, and taking the principle which the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) supported in 1905, we say that Manitoba to-day is entitled to similar compensation in lieu of her public lands to that which was given to Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905 and winch has been enjoyed by both of these provinces ever since.

For the reason that I have already mentioned, we say further that the allowance in respect of public lands ought to date, not from to-day, but from the 1st day of July, 1908. My hon. friend seems to think that there is no precedent for this. There have been a good many precedents for antedating allowances. It was done in the case of Nova Scotia in 1869; it was done in respect of all the provinces in 1884. Nova Scotia under a statute of this parliament passed in 1869 received an allowance, not from 1869, but commencing on the 1st day of July, 1867.

Then it was discovered that instead of the allowance which Canada, that is, Ontario and Quebec, got of $62,000,000, the allowance should have been $73,000,000, and changes were made in respect of other provinces. Canada was paying interest from 1867 upon

$10,000,000 upon which she should not have paid it, and the Act of 1884 provided that the interest payments should be to Canada as of the confederation year. There was a principle for which there was full justification. But surely that is different from this case. Alberta and Saskatchewan weret incorporated five years ago. But leave that out, and come to the year 1908. Since 1908 Alberta and Saskatchewan have been governing and controlling all the territories within their boundaries and have been entitled to the subsidies which we gave them. Manitoba on the other hand, has not been in possession or control of the added territory at all, nor has she spent a five-cent piece or incurred a responsibility there, while on the other hand, she has had possession of the swamp lands, which have been estimated as worth from $25,000,000 to $30,000,000, and has enjoyed !the proceeds of those lands. What would have been done if Manitoba had passed an Act in 1908 accepting the boundary then offered? But she did not do it. Manitoba was in default and not Canada, and why should the treasury of Canada suffer to the extent of $2,000,000 because of that default on the part of Manitoba? That is the ground of my amendment.
